Item 1, bullet point 3: "The problem of unprofessional work of the police was discussed, as well as cases of theft and robbery committed by members of the police, who are imposing themselves as a force and authority unto itself. "It was concluded that more efforts should be invested in preventing and apprehending individuals involved in criminal activities." And point 6: "The service in charge of resettlement is required to set up records in local communes of people who wish to move away and to announce its arrival in any local commune three days in advance." Do you see that already on the next day, they reviewed the issue of unauthorised conduct by certain members of the police force?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the minutes show, although they don't expressly connect it to the question of money taken from those leaving. But they do see the police operating unauthorised. I do tie this into what we see in general. By late July, the crisis staffs -- the police are increasingly saying that they have their own authority, their own chains of command, and the War Presidency's authority over police is resented by the police structures. So we see, perhaps, another side of the coin here, that the War Presidency is resenting the police setting themselves up as a force and authority unto itself. But, yes, they're discussing police committing robberies. They don't connect it to the question of money taken from those leaving, and they are getting more detailed and more organised in their resettlement service in item 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doesn't it mean anything to you that this information about unauthorised confiscation of money was given just the day before, and already that this date that we are looking at, it's being discussed, this unauthorised conduct by police officers?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could well be related. I'm not denying. They could well be related.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1313, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 321, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a session of the War Presidency of the 31st of July, 1992. We see the agenda, the analysis of the conclusions of the Executive Committee, which is already in operation, and then further down it says: "In order to prevent robberies in houses that are abandoned, warehouses need to be established to collect all the goods, that is, movable property, that is at risk of being looted. "The competent committee for sealing apartments and houses is to carry out a check on the persons who have moved into apartments or houses without authorisation and supply the Public Security Station with this list. "In the police station at Siprage, appropriate measures should be taken to prevent unauthorised behaviour by the police." Do you remember that Siprage is a majority Muslim place, and here the War Presidency is demanding that the police act in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I do not know the population of Siprage, but here, yes, I see that the War Presidency is ordering the police to act in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To stop unauthorised conduct by the police. Isn't that an appeal to lawful behaviour, a demand for lawful behaviour?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this previous paragraph, to protect property, it relates to the protection of abandoned property?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it relates to the protection of abandoned property.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be received?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. D1313 -- D1314. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 527, please. The Prosecution attached -- or, rather, put together two different sets of minutes, but we don't mind. On page 1, it says in item 2 that some two members of special units were arrested; that security should be organised for convoys. Convoys are not organised, but security for them is organised. Can we see the next page. The next page says: "The president, N. Djekanovic, informed the Presidency of the visit of the representative of the ICRC and the conversation the night before about the operation of civilian authorities and overcoming some problems that yielded no result." In English, we should have left the previous page on. I'm sorry. The previous page in English: "President Nedeljko Djekanovic." And then it says: "Zdravko Pejic informed the War Presidency about the instructions, that is, the order issued by President Karadzic in connection with resolving the issue of Vecici, and his demand that the civilian population be protected as much as possible."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you include this in your report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you explain why?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was looking at the overall course of events in Kotor Varos and elsewhere, and the pattern I see was the moving out. I do see individual references to humanitarian law, the abiding by the -- I've seen other telegrams from Karadzic for other areas about protecting the civilian population. I've seen this. I probably forwarded it to the trial team as an example of Rule 68. It is certainly -- indicates -- it goes both ways. It indicates communication between Karadzic and the War Presidency, and it certainly says here that he's demanding the civilian population be protected as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in your paragraph 147, you say that in -- Kotor Varos has seen some of the worst violations, and that this was done on the orders of the Government and Presidency of Republika Srpska. So was it not important to include this? Under Rule 68, the Prosecution is under an obligation to disclose exculpatory evidence to the accused, but an unbiased expert is duty-bound to include and cover everything; is it not so?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot possibly include and cover everything. I do not tie -- when I said that about the worst violence, I was thinking of the detention centres and the earlier killings and mass expulsions in Kotor Varos. The Vecici incident in the fall of 1992 was clearly done with a lot of communication with the regional and republican level, also with the Red Cross. There was a lot of discussion that was -- a lot of communication over that particular issue, which wound up with the civilian population being moved out, not protected and kept in its -- in place. The protection here that we see does not apparently extend to keeping the population there. They were moved out eventually. That is a specific incident, Vecici, which is later than most of the pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is this a pattern where the Serb authorities forcibly removed the civilians from Vecici? Is that the model, is that the pattern?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding of Vecici, although I am not familiar with the exact crime base, is that it was surrounded by Serbian forces and, in the end, they were -- the non-Serbs were allowed to move out rather than the civilians being detained. That's my understanding, but I do not claim to know the entire history of events in Vecici. I do know that this is an example when the War Presidency was in close contact with the republican level over the events. I know that some killings followed in early November, and I can't honestly remember whether they were the men of this village or another place in a school. But I do not see the War Presidency here, or the republican level, intervening to calm the situation down to the extent that the people were allowed to stay in their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, indeed. We'll see now how they were detained and how those civilians were treated. Let me just remind you on the next page in the English version, that activities be taken and that an agreement be reached for a setting up bus service from Siprage to Banja Luka -- from Maslovare and Siprage to Banja Luka. So does it not show to you that the authorities are trying to set up public transportation lines with Siprage? It's the third bullet in the English version, that: "Activities and agreement begin for starting two bus lines from Maslovare to Siprage to Banja Luka." Siprage is a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many Muslims were in Siprage at this point in October 1992. Yes, the authorities are setting up transport lines.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Exhibit D1315.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at 65 ter 268. 268. The date is the 28th of August, a session of the War Presidency. Let's look at item 2. It's about the activities of the enemy in the Bilice area - it's a Croatian village - and provocations on the line facing Bastina, another Croatian village. It says the question was asked about issuing a pass to Captain Serdar, who travelled to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic is asked to give us a reference and to speak more slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a minute. It's in the middle of item 2. Could you repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Item 2: "President Djekanovic again informed those present about the issuing of passes, that this is in the exclusive responsibility of the Defence Office and not the War Presidency, and that they should check to see who issued the pass. Chief Tepic reported that he visited the branch station in Siprage and had a meeting with the police, and attended a meeting of civil authorities and leading figures of the local commune. He insisted on an announcement of the names of police officers who have been engaged in unauthorised dealings." And a little bit further down: "A report from the meeting in Siprage was submitted by the chairman of the Executive Committee, Mr. Komljenovic." And further down, it says: "One ambulance should be acquired for the Siprage Local Commune." And again further down: "Organise a joint meeting with influential people from among the Muslims." Next: "Civilian authorities and directors of private and socially-owned enterprises in the Siprage Local Commune must try to overcome mutual disagreements and address open problems more effectively."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this not what you contested, in other words, an effort to make the residents of Siprage feel safe and live more safely?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I have no personal knowledge of the make-up of the population of Siprage, nor the ethnic background of the police officers there. So, yes, if Siprage is a Muslim settlement and there are still a substantial number of Muslims there, yes, this would be an example of a municipality taking care of all its citizens and trying to make them feel secure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1316, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please look at 65 ter 447.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the session of the 17th of September; again, the War Presidency. And in item 2, it says: "The battalion commander, Slobodan Z.," Slobodan Zupljanin, "briefed the War Presidency on the situation on the ground yesterday and last night. He said that there had not been any significant operations yesterday, but an all-out attack on Vrbanjci took place in the morning. A village was also attacked and set alight, and the people who happened to be there were most probably killed." So in the second half of September, people are being killed in the villages around Kotor Varos. In the municipality of Kotor Varos, the villages are torched, and people living there, who happened to be there, were probably killed?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: You inform me that Vrbanjci was not a Serb settlement, so there's -- I can't recall now whether you said it was Muslim or Croat. So, yes, apparently there are still some non-Serbs there, and there's continued fighting. It doesn't specify which other village was attacked and set alight and who was killed. So there are still some non-Serbs at this -- in Kotor Varos. I never said that they expelled everyone. In fact, I make it clear that -- I made it clear in my testimony now that Vecici was an incident in October, so it was not all finished then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Vrbanjci is inhabited by a substantial number of Serbs, and it is obvious that they came under an attack. So this might be a reference to them, that they might have been killed there, but we will look into that later. We will have a demography -- demographic composition of those places, and you should have taken that into account. You should know that, given the type of report that you wrote. Can we look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that it was Serbs that were attacked. It doesn't say who did the attack and who were the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, if the commander of the Serb Army says that they came under an attack in Vrbanjci, well, he probably is not going to report that he attacked his own forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us proceed. It's not for us to speculate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that here, in item 4, it says that some Serbs submit requests for permission to go to Belgrade to study, and a man is asking for the permission to go back to work, and the War Presidency did not give them their approval? And these are Serbs, Milenko Naric and Jelenko Tepic, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, apparently the request comes from the recruiting office, so I would presume a student and somebody working would be military capable, and, therefore, they're not being excused from the military offices -- from their military duties.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1317, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like us to look at 65 ter 446.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the session that took place on the next day, the 18th of September. And in item 2, it says: "The battalion commander, Slobodan Zupljanin, briefed the War Presidency on the situation in the field yesterday and overnight. He stated that during the morning, the village of Serdari was attacked and burned, and it has been established that on that occasion, the remains of 16 bodies were found. It is not known what happened to two people. A woman and a man were taken away, and one soldier was wounded. He noted that the village was not protected by the troops and that the bodies have been gathered and burial has been agreed, most probably in a mass grave. In order to prevent such things from happening again, he proposes that the village of Dolina be evacuated." Do you see here that the village of Serdari had come under attack - we can check in the census and see that it's a Serb village - that 16 people were killed, and that the village had not been secured, it was not guarded by anyone, by the military?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that they describe the attack on Serdari, which is a Serb village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you say that the War Presidency has control over the municipality and the developments on this territory or that this is not the case, that it does not have control?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not have full control. There's been a military attack on a village, so it does not control the entire territory, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1318, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at 65 ter 473.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the session of the 18th of August, 1992. And in item 2, it says that: "Mane Tepic reported about the death of five soldiers and the wounding of one soldier in the Plana village area, and another soldier was wounded in the Ripiste area by extremists. President Djekanovic proposed that the civilians, who are loyal and who are not mounting resistance, should be allowed to remain in their homes." Are you aware of the fact that -- well, you can see here that people are being killed every day in the depth of the Serb-held territory, and President Djekanovic proposes that the civilians, who are not mounting resistance, who are not opening fire, should remain in their homes?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't see it in this document. Do we have the wrong one called up?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 56, that's what we need, in the English version. I think that the Serb text is okay. No, no, it's not. We need 473. Thank you for your warning. I think that we did not have the correct document. It's the 56th session. The ERN number is 0041-5728.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 5738.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 0041-5738. It's 471; that's the 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The date is the 18th of August. Yes, the 56th session. Mane Tepic informed the War Presidency that five soldiers were killed and one wounded in the Plana area by the extremists. So in the depth of the Serb territory. It's not the BH Army; it's the residents of the Kotor Varos municipality. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's -- I'm sorry. Who is doing the attacking, you mean? That is not the BH Army; it's Kotor Varos residents? We don't know who's been doing the attacking here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am telling you that this is rebellion, armed actions launched by the residents, or, rather, ethnic Muslim extremists, in the depth of the Serb territory, far away from the front-lines. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that here. It doesn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Siprage, Plana, Vecici, all those villages are in the depth of the Serb territory, that they are far away from the front-lines?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I say, Vecici was, as I understood, surrounded by Serbian troops, so it becomes a front-line, itself. If you mean it doesn't -- they're not adjacent to the BH-held territory, I don't know the exact layout of the municipality, so I don't know that, their location. But I don't know where Plana and Ripiste are. If you're saying they're deep in the Serb-held part of the municipality, I have no basis to disagree with that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Madam, Vecici became surrounded once a show-down with the terrorists started, but how could they otherwise have left the village of Vecici to kill people mowing their fields? Is it terrorism if extremists in the depth of your territory kill peaceful residents mowing their fields and if they set on fire their houses and barns? Is that terrorism?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, first and foremost, you're disguising giving evidence as a question. Secondly, you're putting facts that are certainly not contained in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see this report, and did you include the contents thereof in your report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read it. I can't remember if I included it. I think I may have read it in the context of someone should go to Teslic to arrange for the transfer of people moving to Muslim territory: "Those who are loyal and not opposing us should be allowed to stay." I discussed the question of the declaration of loyalty in my report, but I don't recall that I included this specifically in my report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1319, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at 65 ter 358.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These are the minutes of the session of the War Presidency. The date is the 10th of October, 1992. Let us look at the penultimate passage, where it says: "Chairman Nedeljko Djekanovic said that an expanded meeting with the representatives of the Croatian villages was held two days ago, and among the attendees were Vojo Kupresanin, Stojan Zupljanin, and the HDZ representatives from Banja Luka. It was agreed that in the next seven days, all people possessing weapons should surrender, that the HVO should be dissolved, that the chances of accomplishing this were realistic, and that efforts would be made to do something similar with the Muslim side." Ms. Hanson, do you see that by the 10th of October, until that date, Croat and Muslim armed groups were still in existence in the depth of the territory in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the depth of the territory, but, yes, I agree with the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you can see that a meeting was held with the parents in Siprage about the beginning of the school year and the problems - could we please move on to the next page in English - problems faced at the beginning of the school year. We know that Siprage is a majority Muslim village. And then in item 4, you can see that there was a request from the Kurjak family to move out, through the agency of UNPROFOR. And the Kurjaks are a very prominent Muslim family. And there was a request by a man known as Muskula. He wanted to be allowed to move to Ravne, but this was denied. So do you agree that the departure was approved on a case-by-case basis? The prominent family, Kurjak, they were allowed to leave, and Muskula, who was obviously a belligerent person, was not given approval to go to Ravne. So it's not about ethnicity; it's about one's character?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that the accused refrain from adding his own interpretation on what's not in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I think Judge Morrison has given the similar advice, Mr. Karadzic. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is: Do you see that the Kurjak family was allowed to leave, and Muskula's request to leave to the village of Ravne was denied?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see these two specific requests dealt with here, but we've seen that the organisation of -- the departing of convoys was not done on a case-by-case basis by the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that the Kurjak family was not allowed to leave and that Muskula was prevented from going to Ravne; is that so?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that. I said I see these two specific requests dealt with, one from the Kurjak family and one from Muskula. I see them dealt with here. But we have seen that there are busloads and busloads and busloads of people who are leaving from Kotor Varos, and the War Presidency is not debating each individual case. Here, they are debating individual requests, but that's not the same thing as the movement of convoys of buses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's time to take a break, the second break for the day. We'll break for half an hour and resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit the last document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1320, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we see 65 ter 311. 311.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a session of the War Presidency of 13 October 1992, and it says that: "The president of the War Presidency, Nedeljko Djekanovic, stressed there were certain problems about the start of the school year, especially in Siprage, that the situation is still not unsatisfactory. He informed those present about the visit of the International Red Cross, their involvement in supervising the procedure and method of moving people out, and stated that there would be more meetings with them and with representatives of the Croatian people. He also proposed that joint talks be conducted and the other members of the War Presidency should be included." It says there's a contract on transportation, and the license for operation for some enterprises being extended. Did you know that the ICRC was involved in supervising the moving out of the population?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see here that they visited. I don't know how involved they were in the earlier months.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be received?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1321, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see 65 ter 527. 527, 103rd session held on the 21st of October --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry. That's Exhibit D01315.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we saw it earlier on today. The 21st of October.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then I must be confused. Let's move on. Can we see 65 ter 711. [In English] I said, Thank you, Madam Sutherland, and that is not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see this meeting held on 25 October 1992, an appeal from the War Presidency, addressed to all those who temporarily removed - in other words, stole - machinery and other property from abandoned houses. It says that: "All persons found in possession of any movable property acquired without valid documentation after the above dead-line will be handed over to the competent court and criminal proceedings will be conducted against them." Number 3: "The War Presidency appeals to all citizens who have information on unlawful removal of property to report this to a competent organ to allow more effective action to be taken in punishing those who have not handed items in by 1st November 1992." Do you know that this appeal was made and there were attempts made to recover what had been stolen?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen this appeal. We've seen mention in the report -- in the minutes of the War Presidency on recovery of stolen property. So, yes, I'm generally aware of it, and I see that it's in keeping with the Presidency decision back from May of 1992 that says that crisis staffs are to dispose of the property of -- abandoned property and property of those who have left. So it's the War Presidency asserting its authority over abandoned property.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this was not achieved by 25 October; otherwise, this appeal need not have been made?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, movable property -- some movable property appears to have been stolen, not fully under the control of the War Presidency, by October 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1322, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 302, please. 302. Serbian page 9, English page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the document, itself, the minutes are in the wrong order, so we are restoring the proper chronology. So the session took place on 25 October. It's the same body. Item 2, paragraph 2: "Captain Slobodan Zupljanin pointed out that there had been no operations and that regular activities were ongoing. Contact had been established with Vecici, and a proposal was made to send a letter on behalf of the War Presidency, offering the evacuation of their women and children to avoid their getting killed. "In connection with this proposal, all the members of the Presidency stated their individual opinions, and the conclusion was adopted to issue a last call for the release of the women and children and all our prisoners, and then to deal with this issue in a military manner." Is this removal of the population or saving people from combat operations?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, it would appear to be saving people from combat operations, although it's not made clear where they're going to be evacuated to and whether they'll be able to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at item 5. We need the next page in English. Sorry, item 3, second paragraph: "Concerning the return of evacuated citizens to their homes, everywhere where it's possible, these people should be returned to their homes. The Executive Committee will establish a board to list abandoned property and make an order inviting all citizens to return abandoned property." So we see here a reference to an order to return these citizens to their homes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's now complete. What I didn't see in the first part, I now see here, that they're going to plan to return them as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see page 6 in Serbian and English page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is from the 28th of October. Item 2, paragraph 2: "Zdravko Pejic informed the War Presidency about the results of the negotiations with the villagers of Vecici and proposed a solution. "The proposed solution was adopted, to accept the evacuation of the civilian population on the condition that prisoners be released, and then for the remaining part to be blocked by the army and destroyed. "All the members of the War Presidency supported the proposed solution to the issue of the Vecici village." So the civilian population is being spared; right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, here the civilian population is being spared. I would just note a difference between the B/C/S and the English, that they talk about the -- [interpretation] list of prisoners. [In English] Yes, as opposed to the release of the hostages in the English. I just note I don't see "hostages" there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We agree, thank you. There are many wrong translations, but it's about releasing our prisoners and their civilians in order to leave this zone which is at risk?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and then destroy the rest.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see page 5 in Serbian, page 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is 29 October. Item 2: "The War Presidency was informed of the situation on the ground by Slobodan Zupljanin and Zdravko Pejic. Zdravko Pejic informed the War Presidency that there was an agreement with Vecici village to evacuate women and children and the imprisoned Serbs on Sunday." That's what we discussed a moment ago, the children and --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents don't seem to be correct. They're not matching.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the 29th of October session is on page 7 of the English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Seven. Thank you, that's correct, 7. Item 2. Thank you. Can we see page 3 in Serbian and page 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once again, I would note that it says "hostages" in English, but simply "prisoners" in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You know the Serbian language. Do you agree there is a difference between "prisoners," "detainees," and "hostages"? Those are three different categories; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was listening to the English, so, I mean, certainly in English there's a difference between "prisoners" and "hostages." But if you could repeat the B/C/S, I can -- I can make a judgement on the B/C/S. But I wasn't listening to you; I was listening to the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you perhaps listen to the Serbian now. Is there a distinction in Serbian between "captive" or "detainee," on the one hand, and "prisoner," on the other? "Captive" is somebody who was taken captive in combat, and "prisoner" is somebody -- [In English] Prisoner and captive. Prisoner, if it should be "prisoner of war" -- [Interpretation] It should be "prisoner of war" as the equivalent of "zarobljenik." It should be specified that it's a prisoner of war, not just "prisoner"?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I raised the issue mostly in relation to the word "hostage" in English, which is "talac" in B/C/S. The nuances of "zarobljenik" and "zatvorenik" in general, yes, "zatvorenik" is a prisoner, "zarobljenik" is someone who has been taken and imprisoned. So a captive is not a bad translation, but I'm not a professional translator and I don't want to get into the nuances of the language. I was pointing out the hostage issue, not the question of "zarobljenik" versus "zatvorenik."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to take advantage of the fact that you know the Serbian language, so you can clarify it. Please look at this document. It's the 1st of November, 1992. Item 1: "President Nedeljko Djekanovic made an introductory statement about the problem of the evacuation of civilians from Vecici, with a view to reaching agreement on this issue, as well as about the problems that have arisen as a consequence of the corps command's prohibition against allowing civilians out of Vecici before all had laid down their arms. He informed the War Presidency about Karadzic's position that civilians should be allowed to move out from Vecici, as well as that conditions should be provided for that. He also informed the Presidency of a written document which he had signed at the corps command, at the request of General Talic, in which Talic distanced himself from the issue of releasing civilians from Vecici. He urged that it was up to the War Presidency to decide whether it would allow the evacuation of civilians while assuming all responsibility for any subsequent consequences, despite General Talic's reservation ..." So you see that Karadzic takes one position and the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, General Talic, takes a different position, and now the War Presidency is supposed to decide about it; is that correct? My question, "Is that correct," was not interpreted.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we see that Talic is distancing himself. He's not taking a position. Karadzic takes one position. Talic is not taking a position, which is perhaps taking another position. And it's up to the War Presidency to decide whether to allow to evacuate civilians. But they're clearly consulting with higher levels, want to get direction from higher levels on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see that they have to decide and they are aware that they would be the ones bearing the consequences?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they're trying to make sure that they are -- that the -- that Karadzic is aware that they're getting direction from the higher level. They're trying to settle this difference between Karadzic and Talic, so they're not -- I don't see them as trying to act completely independently. They're eager for direction, but they know that they have to take the actions on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Remember paragraph 47 of your report -- sorry, 147, where this president of the War Presidency says evacuation was carried out with the consent of the Government and the Presidency of Republika Srpska. Don't you see he's afraid of those consequences, and he invokes Karadzic's position to allow this?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that in the quotation. You mean that in this document here that I see, he's afraid of the consequences, or in the quotation I use in my paragraph, do I see that he's afraid of the consequences? I see that he's eager for it -- to show that it was not just the War Presidency acting on its own initiative, without any contact with the republican level. This specific incident did get a lot more specific attention from the army command and from the president, as we can see, than a lot of earlier moments. I cannot see any other incident that is so -- where the specifics are really checked at every level. I see later in this document here that it says -- the army major says: "If Karadzic had his own solution to the problem, he should issue an order which we would then execute." So the army is similarly acknowledging Karadzic's authority here. Everyone is trying to make sure that they're in agreement on what is to be done, but it is the War Presidency that is taking the specific action on the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see page 1 in Serbian and in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You will see that it's not exactly as you think. Page 1. The 2nd of November - that's the next day - "President Djekanovic" - that's item 2, paragraph 3: "President Djekanovic said that the state of chaos reigning in the city was mostly a consequence of the fact that the authorities were not functioning, and proposed that the Executive Board take the earliest possible measures and prepare a proposal for clamping down on illicit activities and restoring law and order." Item 3: "As part of this item of the agenda, discussing the problem of appropriation of abandoned property, the failure to implement ..." Et cetera, et cetera. Do you agree this refers to the 2nd of November, 1992, and that chaos still reigns in town?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it seems to be specifically in the town, with the problem of soldiers getting drunk. But, yes, they want to restore law and order in the town, but the lieutenant-colonel remarks that the situation in the field was calm, so it doesn't seem to be chaos everywhere. It's a problem of drunken soldiers and breakdown of law and order in the town.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see page 2 in both versions to see how this interim session continued. This was an interim session of the War Presidency. We need the previous page in English. This can't be the right one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's the next page, page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, sorry, it's the next page. Page 3 in English, so how the session continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The extraordinary session of the War Presidency continued with Colonel Bogo Bogojevic informing all those present that he had received explicit orders from General Mladic that no one was allowed to leave Vecici until the unconditional surrender of weapons was completed. "President Djekanovic concluded there were differences between Karadzic's position and Mladic's position and his order with respect to this problem. "Major Trivic declared the position of the corps command that nobody was allowed to leave Vecici until the unconditional surrender of arms was completed, and proposed that this be said to them once again so that they might give thought to the idea of unconditional surrender. He also remarked that President Djekanovic, when talking to Karadzic, should not tell him that his instructions were not being heeded, but to try and convince him that the only right way to solve the issue of Vecici was unconditional surrender, and asked Djekanovic to help --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please slow down. We are not catching the question because we are still --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your speed is too high so that the interpreters couldn't catch up with it. Repeat your last part of your question. I think you read out the last paragraph of the document. We could all read it. So what is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise to the interpreters, but I am under a great deal of pressure. I don't have enough time to examine this witness. And since I am reading, they can read the translation on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So my question to you, Ms. Hanson, is: Do you see that Karadzic wants the civilians to be allowed to go, but the military considers that this would not be a favourable condition and that they advocate a position whereby the Muslim soldiers should surrender their arms or surrender themselves, and that the War Presidency is, in fact, trying to make me accept this, but without letting me know that my instruction has not been implemented?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with your first part of your question, that Karadzic wants the civilians to be allowed to go, but the military wants unconditional surrender. It's the military suggesting to Djekanovic not to tell Karadzic the whole truth, but whether Djekanovic did or didn't follow that military advice, we don't know. So that's the military's advice to Djekanovic there. But certainly there's a disagreement here between the military and Karadzic, and the president of the Kotor Varos War Presidency is talking to Karadzic about the issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Is it clear from this that the civilians want to leave, and that it was envisaged that the civilians could leave, that the Muslim side has accepted that the civilians should leave, but that the Serb side wants the soldiers to leave alongside or at least to surrender their weapons or, indeed, themselves?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but from this I don't see it's clear what the Muslims, in fact, want. And the Serb side is divided. By "Serb side," the War Presidency, and Karadzic seem to want one thing, and the military another. So I see the Serb side is divided, but we don't know here what it is that the Muslims, themselves, want.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, did we not see from the previous documents that negotiations had been held with the Muslims from Vecici, and that they accepted the solution whereby the civilians and our prisoners of war should be evacuated on Sunday?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we saw that in an -- that's what the War Presidency wrote in an earlier document. I thought you were referring to this particular document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1323, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the minutes that are contained in the Prosecution Exhibit 65 ter 302. Can we please have 65 ter 705.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here on the next day, the 3rd of November, we have another session. Item 2, it says: "Captain Zupljanin informed the War Presidency of a report that the soldiers from Vecici have abandoned the village. The population has also left the village and is in Hadzirica Potok." Item 3: "President Nedeljko Djekanovic informed the War Presidency about the communication from the Command of the 1st Banja Luka Corps and a list of persons who wished to returned to Kotor. "He wants to get a decision on the return of money to persons from Zabrdje who registered to move out but have not departed." As you know, Zabrdje is a Croatian village. Now, does this document, in fact, say those who registered as wanting to move out, and they paid for it, and now, since they did not move out, they need to have that money refunded?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that Zabrdje is a Croatian village. I have no basis for knowing that. And Djekanovic is saying the War Presidency should decide whether to return the money. It's not clear that they will, but it seems to be the phrasing. But they have to decide about whether to return the money.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But he wants a decision to be made. That is his demand. The president of the War Presidency is demanding that the decision be made on the refund of that money to those people. Does that sound like forcible evacuation of those people from Zabrdje, given that they obviously could decide on their own whether they wanted to move out or not?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't know why they haven't moved out, and I assume, from the phrasing, that his decision will be positive. So if he's saying, We will return the money, it seems to be, yeah, not persecution to return the money taken, but we don't know why they haven't departed. In fact, we earlier saw the Crisis Staff or War Presidency saying, Some people haven't left and we have to find out why. So we don't know here, nor do we know that people on the list will be allowed to return to Kotor. But, yes, it seems to be here that they are not being forced to move out, these people, from this place.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1324, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 720, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is dated the 7th of November, another session of the same War Presidency. Item 2: "Lieutenant-Colonel Novakovic briefed the War Presidency on the situation in the field yesterday and stated that the situation was quiet and that the terrain is being combed daily, and features used by the enemy are being discovered. He also informed the War Presidency that yesterday troops went into Vecici and captured three members of the Green Berets." Did you have this document at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D1325, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 333, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is dated the 12th of November. Item 2 or paragraph 2: "Colonel Novakovic stressed that the situation was peaceful, except for the fact that there was some shooting from the village of Dulici on Kalamande, that there is a great deal of fear there and people are demanding evacuation. He proposed that somebody go out into the field and see how to deal with this." Kalamande is a Serb village and Dulici is a Croatian village; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I note that the English was not correct. It's a different session up in the English. And I have absolutely no basis for saying the ethnic make-up of Dulici and Kalamande.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the English version we need 123, page 123, not 22, as it is now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you speak Serbian, and do you agree -- next page in the English version. Yes, 123, that's the one. Well, is this a correct translation, that the situation was calm, except that there was shooting from the area around the village of Dulici towards Kalamande?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we go back to page -- or, rather, to the 122nd session, both in English and in Serbian. That's the previous one. The English is good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here, item 2: "President Djekanovic reported to the War Presidency on the results of the meeting with General Talic which was held yesterday in Doboj. In connection with certain issues, the general suggested the following: that all irresponsible and undisciplined soldiers and mercenaries be detained and sent to the front-line near Orasje." And further down: "In the area of Siprage, there should be no activities that could possibly aggravate the situation." And then: "In addition to the much-needed Serbian conscripts, the work obligation should be imposed on retired people and a certain percentage of other nationalities." Do you know that the right to assign work obligation is defined by an appropriate law?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the specific law, but I know that it was a legal concept, yes. The work obligation is to make people stay in their employment or to give them employment -- make them work at times of emergencies, in general, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the document, itself, do you agree that the word "mercenary" was used instead of "loose cannon," which was the Serbian word used by General Talic? Item 2, first bullet point.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian is "slobodni strelci," "free shooters." I don't know if that has a specific military meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Slobodni strelci" means "uncontrolled elements," those who act as they see fit. Well, do you know that this would be in the spirit of the Serbian language, that "loose cannon" would be a much better translation, somebody who is out of control and who's acting of their own free will?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not familiar with the phrase, so I don't know its connotations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that in the area of Siprage, General Talic suggested that nothing should be done that could aggravate the situation and raise the tensions there?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last page, the last paragraph: "The issues of bus lines in Kotor Varos and Maslovare and Siprage area, and the power supply, were discussed." Do you see that these authorities are dealing with the Muslim population living in Siprage in a highly-responsible manner?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't see it in this -- oh, at the very end. Yes, now I see it. Once again, all I know say is I don't know the make-up of Siprage or Maslovare at this time, but I see that they are working on typical municipal affairs, such as bus lines and electrical energy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if there is enough time, we will present the census data to see who lived in what village. Can this please be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1326, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, I've spent two and a half sessions to try to prove that your position -- your conclusion in paragraph 147, that Kotor Varos is the municipality that witnessed some of the worst violations, is not correct. Do you have any other document that would run contrary to the documents that I presented which all show that there were responsible authorities operating there? Do you have anything that would support your position?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have documents where the Crisis Staff sets up the sawmill detention centre. The minutes of the Crisis Staff/War Presidency, themselves, do not describe what went on, nor do they describe in detail why busloads and busloads and busloads of people were shipped out, why they wanted to leave. So the documents of Kotor Varos War Presidency, itself, do not describe the wider situation on the ground, the kind of fighting, the kind of acts that were going on that drove people to leave. So the "worst violations" phrase, I agree, is not -- is not supported by the documents there. It was just from a general understanding of events in Bosnia. What I am emphasizing is here that the departure of hundreds -- thousands of people was organised by the municipal authorities, that they regarded themselves as acting in accordance with the laws and the instructions of their republic, that they contacted the republic level where necessary. For this one issue of Vecici, there was a lot of attention and lot of communication with the republican level. But the minutes of the crisis staffs/war presidencies, themselves, do not detail the actions taken against Muslims and Croats and what those people were suffering that led them to seek to depart in mass numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, based on what documents did you conclude that the worst violations of rights were committed there, if that is not contained in the documents of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, that would be outside documents in my report, just my understanding of the crimes -- the events on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Hanson, we have a problem, then, with your understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed. I was about to ask that, What did you base your understanding on? Please continue, Mr. Karadzic. I didn't want to intervene in your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome to it. Please intervene as often as you feel like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, do you know that by that time, at least three agreements were reached by the warring factions in Bosnia and Herzegovina, agreements allowing free resettlement of the population, including the obligation on the part of the municipal authorities to secure the convoys? On the 22nd of May, in late July, in late August, and the fourth one on the 30th of September and the 1st of October, agreements were signed to ensure that the population could be resettled in the areas where they felt safe, and the municipal authorities were under an obligation to secure the convoys?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not specifically aware of those agreements, but I would -- when you say "free resettlement," I don't think it applies to the kind of resettlement we're talking about here where it's free and voluntary and simply moving them to a safe location. The point is that the movement -- the mass movement of populations -- the phrase "free resettlement" implies it's entirely voluntary, and that is not what I'm talking about when I talk about forcible removal. As for the obligation to secure the convoys, I do see lots of documents of municipal authorities securing the convoys, but not an equal attention paid to the security of the population in-situ. The non-Serb population, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, I thought Mr. Karadzic would ask that question. In response to the last question of Mr. Karadzic as to the basis for the conclusion in the last paragraph, i.e., paragraph 147, you answered that: "It would be outside documents in my report, just my understanding of the crimes, the events on the ground." Could you expand on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite aside from my work on this memo, which became an expert report, I and my team, we researched a lot of different topics and were familiar with the findings and the investigations. So I know that we have a report on the various municipalities, our understanding of events in municipalities. I have access to a lot of different documents, so it's part of my job to know, in general, the pattern. When I look at something specifically like the issue of crisis staffs, I would cite every document that I feel relevant, but I already have a framework for understanding events. And I think I was thinking of the detention centres and some killings that I knew of there. Perhaps -- I mean, I don't say that it was the worst, but I know that -- I know that some -- there were some very bad killings and detention centres in Kotor Varos, and that was on my mind, that it was not -- it was not a municipality untouched by war. Perhaps the phrase "some of the worst" is too rhetorical. I mean, I wouldn't want to list the municipalities, in terms of which was the worst, but if I would say the top 10, I think Kotor Varos would be up there. It certainly would not be one of the most peaceful municipalities. I was emphasizing there the communications with the top level, that the War Presidency was not acting on its own, was not considering itself an independent organ, untied to the republic level, but I did not, as you see, try and examine each crime base and connect each crisis staff to each crime base. I was more describing, in general, what crisis staffs did. And where I know that crimes were committed or killings occurred, detention centres occurred, forcible removals occurred, I would consider that some of the violence to which I refer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When you refer to reports or documents, would those include statements of witnesses or a summary of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In general, no. I don't have a lot to do with witness statements, and I don't use them as a basis of my memos. I certainly come across them, yes, in the course of my research, but I and my team really base ourselves on the documents, not witness work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ma'am, we'll have to get back to this. Thank you, Your Excellency, for this clarification that was elicited, and it makes my job easier. I don't have that much experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in your report that one of the municipalities that forcibly removed non-Serbs was Bosanski Petrovac; in other words, that Bosanski Petrovac was one of those municipalities. I don't know if this has been interpreted. I would kindly ask you to interpret everything that I am saying.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear a question interpreted. I discussed the actions of the Petrovac Crisis Staff. Certainly, it matches the pattern of setting up agencies, having people who want to leave sign a form stating that they are leaving their property to the state. So, I discuss it, yes, in the section on the removal of population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in paragraph 95, you couch it in much harsher terms. Let me read: [In English] "To protect the interests of the Serbs, crisis staffs ensured Serb power on the ground by enabling the persecution and forcible removal of non-Serbs." [Interpretation] And then in paragraph 96, you say: [In English] "Crisis staffs ordered the arrest of individuals and whole categories of people, such as all people of Croatian nationality in Bosanski Samac or all military-capable Muslims who could possibly harm the Serbs in Bosanski Petrovac." [Interpretation] Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what my report says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 100, you say: [In English] "The Crisis Staffs oversaw the removal of non-Serbs from the municipalities by establishing 'committees for emigration,' 'travel agencies' and 'exchange agencies.' When a delegation of Muslims inquired of the War Commission in Bosanski Petrovac whether the Muslims would have a guarantee of safety in the municipality, the War Commission responded by forming a commission for the departure of the Muslims." So those crisis staffs in Kotor Varos and in Bosanski Petrovac, and in probably other municipalities, are accused by you not that they enabled people to leave, if they wished, but that they forcibly drove out Muslims and Croats from their municipalities, is that correct, and you give selectively two or three documents, leaving out a mass of documents that create or provide a completely different broader picture; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second half of your sentence -- your question, or your second question, no, I don't agree that I leave out a mass of documents that don't -- that show a different picture. I -- the quotation I give, these Muslims went to the War Commission, they said, Can you guarantee our safety? And the War Commission's response was to form a commission for them to leave. I take that as a pretty clear action, We're not going to guarantee your safety, but we will allow you to leave in an organised way, provided you leave your property to the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they say, We won't, or, We can't because the municipality is too large? These small distortions, Ms. Hanson, are they something an unbiased expert witness is allowed to make?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't say, "we can't," they didn't say, "we won't." Their answer was to form a commission for mass emigration or a commission for the departure of Muslims. That was their answer. Because the municipality is too large, I don't see that saying that at all. If we can look at the document, we can see what --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 65 ter 1062. Let's move to Bosanski Petrovac, although both these municipalities are now out of the indictment, but you describe them in your report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know whether Mr. Karadzic is going to show Ms. Hanson that document or whether he wants me to deal with it in redirect. She asked to look at the document, which was 65 ter 1115.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The time will come. We'll come to that, Madam Sutherland, and there will be also your redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question with your microphone on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't asked my question yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here is the question: This is a session of the Crisis Staff of 24 May 1992. Item 2: "The president read the order on general mobilisation in the Serbian Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina and made an introductory statement thereon. Mr. Miljevic submitted a report about the coverage of military conscripts by mobilisation, stressing that for the most part, all military-capable citizens have already been engaged on one or another basis and that mobilisation in our municipality has been carried out even before this order."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please slow down when reading out documents. And do we have the proper English page now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you see that everyone who could possibly be engaged has been engaged already, and the representative of the 2nd Corps thinks it is now pointless to talk about plans because all plans were practically invalidated by the factual situation. He stressed the need to immediately implement civil order and military discipline. Can we see the Serbian page 2 and English 2, because we need item 3. Item 3 of the order relates to the imposition of order and prevention of looting of military, private, and social property. Can we see item 3 in Serbian, and the next page in English, probably. Item 3 in Serbian. Military police organs of the Public Security Station are ordered to prevent looting. This is the month of May, a month and a half into the war. Did you take into account these efforts to prevent looting, including looting of private property?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It should be page 3 in English and the previous page in Serbian as well, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Point 3. Very early on the 24th of May, an order is given to all forces, both civilian and military police, to be engaged in preventing looting?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not include this in my report. I see that as part of the regular work of crisis staffs, but I didn't -- I didn't -- couldn't possibly cover every single thing that crisis staffs dealt with. I covered the issues that I considered relevant to the needs of the trial team. I mean, I could -- as I said before, I could have done everything on fuel and commodity reserves, or here the -- so looting, but it doesn't -- the issues that I was looking at were more specific, those, you know, of my terms of reference. That's why I wouldn't include everything that crisis staffs did or dealt with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see item 2, where it says that ethnic Muslims, members of the Muslim community, will be engaged in companies and organisations? In other words, it means they will not be mobilised; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's no reference to them not being mobilised. It says that the companies can request. I mean, they will be employed if the companies that employ them request it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In item 3, do you see that through the mass media: "... information will be made public about the Military Court starting to work, with a seat in Drvar; it shall be emphasised that all persons who violate the rules, and especially those caught in the act or proven to be guilty of stealing, looting, et cetera shall be severely punished." The last sentence: "Very harsh verdicts will be meted out and implemented immediately." Did you include this in your report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1327, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Five minutes for today, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 65 ter 1068, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Minutes of the 28th May. Item 1: Dragan Milanovic. He was an assistant to the deputy to the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina: "Dragan Milanovic informed the Crisis Staff about the results, the outcome of his talks with representatives of the citizens' forum of the SDA. Representatives of the SDA, Safet Hidic and Mustafa Ferizovic, are spreading alarming rumours among Muslim citizens by saying that the Muslim citizens want to emigrate collectively. However, according to Dragan Ivanic, the citizens' forum has a unanimous stand with respect to Muslims being loyal citizens and supporting the authorities. They accuse Safet Hidic and Mustafa Ferizovic of illegal arming and say that the citizens' forum is prepared to take part in solving the refugee problems, together with other citizens, and that they are ready for the mobilisation; also, that they say they will try to find out the names of the people who are being trained to become members of the Green Berets."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Slow down, slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is almost the end of the second month of the war, in May. Did you include in your report this document, which speaks of the talks with the citizens' forum, normal, regular citizens who distanced themselves from extremists?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not include this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have an explanation why, why you did not include such a striking example of the care authorities took on their own citizens?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you compare this to the document I did include of, We should arrest all military-capable Muslims who could possibly harm the Serbs, I have to strike a balance. Which is more plausible, which is it a better reflection of the situation. Petrovac was, as I recall, one of the most thoroughly Serb municipalities, very few Muslims. Not surprising that the Muslims who were there are eager to demonstrate their loyalty and stay, if they can, because they are outnumbered. I don't show every document where crisis staffs are not doing bad things. The question is: What did they do, and did they -- what was their role in the state, was the essential questions of my report. So when a municipal authority is prepared to protect its own people, that is, to my mind, the municipal authority doing its job, regardless of the nationality of its citizens. The problem is when the municipal authority is -- says its job is to defend the interests of only one ethnic group and it has other citizens in its territory.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll come to that. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1328, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And adjourn for today. Tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm kindly you asking for additional time. If I can get Friday too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. You have about two and a half -- between two and a half and three hours left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am asking for Friday too, because the Prosecution spent double time than they announced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not correct. We had 2.5 hours in the schedule, and I took, I think, approximately 3.5 hours. So it was additional time, but not double.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tomorrow, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: reconvened on Wednesday, the 15th day of June, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.
